description: Fawcett, the Pankhursts, Emily Davison and the long campaign that won women the vote in 1918.
content_html:
The Campaign for Women’s Votes

Women in Britain paid taxes, ran businesses and raised families, but were excluded entirely from voting in parliamentary elections. By 1897 a moderate campaign for women’s suffrage — the right to vote — had been building for over thirty years. Women's suffrage was debated in Parliament as early as 1867, when John Stuart Mill proposed an amendment to extend the vote to women. It was defeated, but the debate never went away.

Key Fact

The National Union of Women’s Suffrage Societies (NUWSS), founded in 1897 and led by Millicent Fawcett, campaigned through legal, peaceful means: petitions, public meetings and lobbying Parliament.

The Suffragists: NUWSS

Millicent Fawcett became president of the NUWSS in 1897 and led it for over twenty years. The Suffragists (as members of the NUWSS were known) believed in working within the law. They organised peaceful demonstrations, collected hundreds of thousands of petition signatures, and lobbied sympathetic MPs. By 1913 the NUWSS had around 54,000 members, organised in over 400 local societies. Fawcett argued that women’s capacity for rational argument was the best proof that they deserved the vote — and that violent tactics would undermine the cause.

The Suffragists made real but slow progress. Several private members’ bills to extend the vote to women came close to passing in the early 1900s but were blocked or talked out. Prime Minister Asquith was personally opposed to women’s suffrage, and the Liberal government, despite its progressive credentials, refused to act.

The Suffragettes: WSPU

Frustrated by inaction, Emmeline Pankhurst founded the Women’s Social and Political Union (WSPU) in Manchester in 1903 alongside her daughters Christabel and Sylvia. The WSPU’s motto was “Deeds, not words.” At first the WSPU pursued peaceful methods alongside the NUWSS, but from 1908 it escalated to increasingly militant tactics: smashing windows, chaining themselves to railings, setting fire to post boxes and empty buildings, and disrupting public meetings.

When arrested, Suffragettes mounted hunger strikes in prison to force the government to release them or risk the scandal of a campaigner dying in custody. The government responded in 1913 with the Cat and Mouse Act, which allowed hunger-striking prisoners to be released until they recovered their health and then re-arrested. Critics called it inhumane and designed to keep women in a permanent state of legal jeopardy without the martyrdom of a prison death.

Emily Davison was a committed Suffragette who had been imprisoned multiple times and force-fed during hunger strikes. On 4 June 1913 she ran onto the racecourse at the Epsom Derby and was struck by the King’s horse, Anmer. She died from her injuries four days later. Her funeral procession through London was attended by tens of thousands of supporters. Historians debate her intentions: some argue she intended to attach a WSPU banner to the horse as a protest; others believe she intended to die for the cause. Either way, her death drew international attention to women’s suffrage.

Key Fact

The Cat and Mouse Act 1913 allowed the government to release hunger-striking Suffragettes temporarily when they became seriously ill, then re-arrest them when they recovered. It was designed to prevent a Suffragette dying in custody and becoming a martyr.

Divisions Within the Campaign

The WSPU was increasingly dominated by Emmeline and Christabel Pankhurst, who ruled it autocratically. Sylvia Pankhurst was eventually expelled for her socialist and working-class focus, which conflicted with the WSPU’s increasingly narrow middle-class emphasis. The NUWSS and WSPU also disagreed fundamentally on tactics: Fawcett consistently argued that violence and property destruction alienated public sympathy and gave opponents grounds to deny women the vote on the basis that they were “irrational.”

The First World War and the 1918 Act

When war broke out in August 1914, both the NUWSS and the WSPU suspended their campaigns. Emmeline and Christabel Pankhurst actively encouraged women to support the war effort and pressure men to enlist — a dramatic reversal that caused a split with Sylvia Pankhurst, who opposed the war. During the war, women took on vital roles — in munitions factories, as nurses, as land army workers, and in transport — that made it almost impossible to sustain the argument that they were unfit to vote.

The Representation of the People Act 1918 gave the vote to women aged 30 and over who met a property qualification, enfranchising approximately 8.4 million women. Men over 21 received the vote without property qualification. Full equal voting rights for women — voting at 21 on the same terms as men — came only with the Equal Franchise Act 1928.

Historians debate which factors mattered most. The Suffragette view emphasises that militancy forced the government to act. But the age and property restrictions in the 1918 Act suggest the government had not fully accepted equality — they deliberately excluded young working-class women who had done most of the war work. The Suffragist view emphasises that the NUWSS’s patient lobbying and the wartime service of women together created the political conditions for reform. It is most accurate to see the 1918 Act as the product of long-term constitutional pressure (NUWSS), changed attitudes from wartime service, and the political inconvenience of continuing to exclude women once millions of men had also been disenfranchised by the loss of the residential qualification during the war.
exam_tip_html: For ‘Explain a Cause’ or ‘Explain a Consequence’ questions on women’s suffrage, be precise: name the specific organisation (NUWSS or WSPU), date, and tactic. For 12-mark ‘Evaluate an Interpretation’ questions, a common one is whether militancy or constitutional campaigning was more important. Always include both — agree and disagree — before reaching your own substantiated judgement. Avoid the trap of only describing what happened instead of explaining why it mattered.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The NUWSS (Suffragists), led by Millicent Fawcett from 1897, used peaceful constitutional methods. The WSPU (Suffragettes), led by Emmeline Pankhurst from 1903, escalated to militancy from 1908, including arson, window-smashing and hunger strikes.
  • Emily Davison died at the 1913 Epsom Derby, becoming the movement’s most prominent martyr. The Cat and Mouse Act 1913 was the government’s attempt to defuse hunger strikes without creating martyrs.
  • The Representation of the People Act 1918 gave the vote to women over 30 with a property qualification (~8.4 million women). Full equal suffrage came only in 1928.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Women's Social and Political Union (WSPU).
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks for a developed point. Example: The WSPU used militant tactics (1), including window-smashing, arson of post boxes and hunger strikes in prison, to pressure the government (1). Mastering: accurate feature with supporting detail. Developing: feature stated but undeveloped.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the campaign of the National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies (NUWSS).
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Feature examples: peaceful and constitutional methods only; petitions with hundreds of thousands of signatures; lobbying sympathetic MPs; public meetings; by 1913 had ~54,000 members in 400+ local societies; led by Millicent Fawcett. Mastering: two precise features with accurate detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the WSPU adopted increasingly militant tactics after 1908.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): Frustration at the failure of peaceful methods — several private members' bills had come close to passing but been blocked; Asquith personally opposed women's suffrage; the Liberal government, despite progressive credentials, repeatedly refused to act; the Suffragettes concluded that peaceful petitioning was insufficient to force change on an obstinate government. Secure (3–4): clear cause with some development. Developing (1–2): simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Emily Davison's death at the 1913 Epsom Derby.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): Her death drew massive international attention to women's suffrage; her funeral procession through London attracted tens of thousands of supporters and was widely reported; it created a powerful martyr figure for the WSPU; it hardened both pro- and anti-suffrage opinion — some were moved by her sacrifice, while opponents used the incident to argue that militancy was irrational and dangerous. Secure (3–4): clear consequence with development. Developing (1–2): simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of women's wartime service (1914–1918) for the women's suffrage movement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8): At the time: women in munitions, nursing, land army and transport made the argument that they were unfit to vote almost impossible to sustain; politicians on all sides acknowledged women's contribution. Over time: directly contributed to the Representation of the People Act 1918 granting votes to women over 30; established the precedent that led to equal suffrage in 1928; transformed the social role of women and expectations about gender equality throughout the twentieth century. Secure (5–6): both dimensions with development. Developing (3–4): mainly one dimension. Emerging (1–2): simple assertion.

practice_questions.text: 'Militant tactics were the main reason women won the vote in 1918.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): Agrees and disagrees, substantiated, overall judgement. Agree: WSPU militancy kept suffrage in public debate; embarrassed the government; martyrdom of Davison and prison hunger strikes attracted sympathy; forced the issue before the war. Disagree: the 1918 Act was triggered by the wartime electoral register problem (men lost residence qualification); women's wartime service changed political opinion; the age restriction (30+, not 21) suggests government was rewarding service not responding to militancy; NUWSS's patient lobbying created the legal and political groundwork. Balanced judgement: militancy maintained the campaign's profile but wartime service and the NUWSS's constitutional work were arguably more decisive in 1918. Secure (7–9): both arguments with development. Developing (4–6): limited. Emerging (1–3): one-sided.

right: WSPU leader who championed 'Deeds, not words'
Suffragette who died after the 1913 Epsom Derby protest

flashcard_questions.q: What did WSPU stand for, and when was it founded?
flashcard_questions.a: Women's Social and Political Union, founded 1903.

flashcard_questions.q: When did the WSPU escalate to militant tactics such as arson and window-smashing?
What happened to Emily Davison at the 1913 Epsom Derby?
flashcard_questions.a: She was struck by a horse and died four days later, becoming the movement's most prominent martyr.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Cat and Mouse Act of 1913?
flashcard_questions.a: It allowed hunger-striking Suffragettes to be released until they recovered, then re-arrested.

flashcard_questions.q: When were women first given the right to vote in British parliamentary elections?
flashcard_questions.a: 1918, under the Representation of the People Act.

flashcard_questions.q: What age and qualification did women need to vote under the 1918 Act?
flashcard_questions.a: Aged 30 or over with a property qualification.

flashcard_questions.q: When did women gain equal voting rights to men in Britain?
Approximately how many women were enfranchised by the 1918 Act?
Why did the NUWSS and WSPU disagree over tactics?
flashcard_questions.a: NUWSS argued militancy alienated public sympathy; WSPU believed constitutional methods were too slow.

flashcard_questions.q: What role did Sylvia Pankhurst take that led to her expulsion from the WSPU?
flashcard_questions.a: She focused on working-class and socialist suffrage, conflicting with the WSPU's middle-class direction.

glossary_terms.definition: The right of women to vote in parliamentary elections, the central demand of both the Suffragists and Suffragettes.
President of the NUWSS (1897–1919), who led the peaceful constitutional campaign for women's votes for over two decades.
Founder and leader of the WSPU from 1903, who championed militant suffragette tactics including arson, window-smashing and hunger strikes.
The 1913 Prisoners (Temporary Discharge for Ill-Health) Act that allowed hunger-striking prisoners to be released temporarily and re-arrested when recovered.
Suffragette (1872–1913) who died after being struck by a horse at the 1913 Epsom Derby, becoming the most prominent martyr of the suffragette movement.
The Act that gave the vote to women aged 30 or over with a property qualification, enfranchising approximately 8.4 million women.
